workspace\027-全村的希望-fd28f325c70f\applications\github-stage-1\.haiknow\acceptance.json:10:      "source_quote": "The registration page is the form opened by the unique link named “Create an account” from the sign-in page. The form contains exactly one textbox labeled “Username”, one textbox labeled “Email”, one password input labeled “Password”, one password input labeled “Confirm password”, one initially unchecked checkbox named “Agree to the terms”, and one enabled button named “Create account”. The username and email identify the account, while passwords must not be echoed on the page. This product directly marks the email of a successfully registered account as verified and does not provide a subsequent email-verification page. The visitor enters a unique username, email, password, and matching confirmation, checks “Agree to the terms”, and activates “Create account”. The username must consist of 1 to 39 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, or single hyphens (`-`) and must not begin or end with a hyphen; after trimming leading and trailing whitespace, the email must contain exactly one `@`, be no longer than 254 characters, and have at least one dot and non-empty domain labels after the `@`; the password must contain 12 to 128 characters, include at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one digit, and one non-alphanumeric special character, and contain no whitespace characters. The system stores a sign-in-capable account together with its verified-email status and enters the sign-in page; if the username or email conflicts, any field is missing, the email format is invalid, the terms are not accepted, the password is noncompliant, or the confirmation does not match, the system retains the username and email input, displays an itemized message beside the corresponding field, and does not create an account. The corresponding visible field message contains “Username already exists”, “Username format is invalid”, “Email format is invalid”, “Password requirements are not satisfied”, or “Agree to terms is required”, as applicable. Visitors can use this capability on the account-access page. The system validates input rules, displays field errors, and prevents duplicate accounts; on success, it directly creates an available account. Submitting several invalid fields together must show the username, email, password, and missing-terms messages together, rather than revealing only one error per submission; the submit button remains actionable so these messages can be read. For example, a username beginning with a hyphen, email “not-an-email”, password “short”, confirmation “different”, and unchecked terms produce these field errors and preserve the attempted username. A duplicate username paired with a different unused email displays “Username already exists” and retains both attempted values. A successful registration accepts a unique username, its email, and password; the sign-in form is immediately available, accepts that email, and the resulting signed-in username remains visible after reload.

2"},{"req_id":"ROOT","path":"fields.description","text":"This product is a simplified GitHub collaboration platform. Unless an atomic requirement explicitly allows more than one role, every quoted user-interface name is the exact English accessible name of the control; the role, scope, and observable-state rules stated by each atomic requirement are authoritative. Values described as existing accounts, organizations, teams, repositories, branches, files, commits, issues, milestones, pull requests, reviews, and permission relationships are predefined seed data. The application must provision those records before the corresponding scenario and supply each account through an isolated browser session; they are not extra features that a participant must expose through a private API. Generated names may contain a unique suffix, but their role, ownership, visibility, and relationships are exactly those stated in the atomic requirement. Every atomic requirement remains enabled even when seed configuration is incomplete. Organization Owner, repository Admin, Read, Triage, Write, Maintain, and Admin permissions follow the operation-specific rules in the requirements below; these roles are not an automatic cumulative ladder. Real-time collaboration, Actions, Packages, Wiki, project boards, notification delivery, and external Git remote protocols are outside the scope of this product."},{"req_id":"REQ-3","path":"fields.name","text":"Repository Asset Management"},{"req_id":"REQ-3","path":"fields.description","text":"A repository is a container for code, branches, commits, files, and collaborative work items. The repository overview page is titled “owner/repository name”, displays the owner, name, Public/Private marker, description, and default branch, and provides Code, Issues, Pull requests, and Settings entries; the “owner” is an individual account or organization, and a repository belonging to an organization is an organization repository. Users open a repository overview from global search results, a personal/organization Repositories list, or a direct link; signed-in users with creation permission create a personal or organization repository from “New repository”. Public repositories allow visitor Read access; private personal repositories allow access only to their owner and explicitly authorized subjects; private organization repositories allow access only to organization Owners, members with direct repository roles, or direct members of teams with repository roles, and ordinary organization Members do not automatically gain access merely through membership. After visibility or access grants change, search, lists, direct links, and repository pages must all use the same access rule."},{"req_id":"REQ-3-1","path":"fields.name","text":"Search for and Locate Repositories"},{"req_id":"REQ-3-1","path":"fields.description","text":"The top global search control has searchbox role and accessible name “Search”; entering a repository name and pressing Enter displays repository results directly, without requiring an additional type-filter click. Each repository result has a link whose accessible name is exactly its repository name, while the result also displays its owner/name metadata. Clicking it opens a heading containing the repository name; reloading preserves that overview. A query with no matching repository displays “No results”, including when the visitor returns home and repeats the same query. Seed data provides a named public repository and a private repository inaccessible to visitors; searching the private name exposes no result link for it. Visitors or signed-in users can search repositories they are authorized to view. The system accepts a search query, applies repository-oriented filters or scope constraints, and displays matching repositories with sufficient metadata for the user to open the target repository.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-repository-search-results.png)"},{"req_id":"REQ-3-2","path":"fields.name","text":"Repository Creation and Distribution"},{"req_id":"REQ-3-2","path":"fields.description","text":"The repository-creation page is the form opened by “New repository”, where the user selects an owner, name, visibility, and initialization options. A “fork” is an independent repository copied from a readable source repository — the frontend displays the source link on the fork overview page, and the system stores the source-repository identifier; branches and commits in the fork may evolve independently and never write back to the source repository. A “clone page entry” is a read-only address displayed in the repository Code popover and can be copied to the clipboard; it does not mean this product implements an external Git protocol. Both new repositories and forks must enter a browsable repository overview page. This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes."},{"req_id":"REQ-3-2-1","path":"fields.name","text":"Create a Repository with Owner, Visibility, and Initialization Options"},{"req_id":"REQ-3-2-1","path":"fields.description","text":"This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes. The signed-in workspace provides a “New repository” link. The form labels are “Owner”, “Repository name”, and “Description”; the signed-in user's personal namespace is selected by default, so it is possible to submit without changing the owner. Visibility choices are radio controls “Public” and “Private”; initialization is a checkbox “Add a README file”; submission uses the button “Create repository”. Other defaults must allow duplicate-name and empty-name validation without further input. A successful initialized private repository shows a heading containing the new name, a visible Private marker, and a README file link; the overview persists after reload. The optional description “Repository created by Playwright” is saved when entered. An existing repository in this same default personal namespace is supplied for duplicate validation, which stays on the form and does not open the existing repository heading. On the repository-creation page, a signed-in user selects a personal or organization owner, enters a repository name and description, selects public or private visibility, and chooses whether to create an initial commit with a README. The system verifies that the user may create a repository in that owner's namespace, that the name is unique, and that the options are valid; on success, it stores the repository identifier, owner, visibility, default branch, and creator. If initialization is selected, it must also atomically create the initial branch, README file, and initial commit; failure at any step must leave no partially created repository. On success, the new repository overview page is opened.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-create-repository.png)"},{"req_id":"REQ-3-2-2","path":"fields.name","text":"Fork a Repository into Another Namespace"},{"req_id":"REQ-3-2-2","path":"fields.description","text":"The source overview has a button “Fork”. The fork form contains a field labeled “Repository name” and button “Create fork”; it defaults to the signed-in user's personal namespace and an allowed visibility, permitting submission after editing only the name. Seed data supplies a readable source, a user allowed to create personal repositories, and an existing fork name in that namespace for the conflict case. Success opens a heading containing the new fork name and visible text “Forked from <source repository name>” with a source link; the heading and source relationship survive reload. On the source repository page, the user clicks “Fork”, selects a target personal or organization namespace, enters an optional new name and visibility, and clicks “Create fork”. The system creates an independent fork, copies the accessible default-branch history, records the source-repository link, and then opens the new fork overview page. This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes. A signed-in user can fork only when they have Read or higher permission on the source repository and permission to create repositories in the target personal or organization namespace; when the source repository is private, the fork must remain Private, while a public source repository may be forked as Public or Private. The system validates permissions on both ends and stores the new fork's owner, visibility, source-repository identifier, default branch, and copied accessible history; if any check fails, no fork is created.

The fork conflict seed uses the existing name `acme-docs-fork` in the target
personal namespace.

Each tab provides a button for copying the selected clone value. With browser clipboard permission, the visitor can copy the selected value, receives brief “Copied” feedback, and continues to see the repository heading. This read-only operation does not modify the repository. The capability builds on the public repository overview provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview) and is available to a visitor who can view that repository.

2"},{"req_id":"ROOT","path":"fields.description","text":"This product is a simplified GitHub collaboration platform. Unless an atomic requirement explicitly allows more than one role, every quoted user-interface name is the exact English accessible name of the control; the role, scope, and observable-state rules stated by each atomic requirement are authoritative. Values described as existing accounts, organizations, teams, repositories, branches, files, commits, issues, milestones, pull requests, reviews, and permission relationships are predefined seed data. The application must provision those records before the corresponding scenario and supply each account through an isolated browser session; they are not extra features that a participant must expose through a private API. Generated names may contain a unique suffix, but their role, ownership, visibility, and relationships are exactly those stated in the atomic requirement. Every atomic requirement remains enabled even when seed configuration is incomplete. Organization Owner, repository Admin, Read, Triage, Write, Maintain, and Admin permissions follow the operation-specific rules in the requirements below; these roles are not an automatic cumulative ladder. Real-time collaboration, Actions, Packages, Wiki, project boards, notification delivery, and external Git remote protocols are outside the scope of this product."},{"req_id":"REQ-3","path":"fields.name","text":"Repository Asset Management"},{"req_id":"REQ-3","path":"fields.description","text":"A repository is a container for code, branches, commits, files, and collaborative work items. The repository overview page is titled “owner/repository name”, displays the owner, name, Public/Private marker, description, and default branch, and provides Code, Issues, Pull requests, and Settings entries; the “owner” is an individual account or organization, and a repository belonging to an organization is an organization repository. Users open a repository overview from global search results, a personal/organization Repositories list, or a direct link; signed-in users with creation permission create a personal or organization repository from “New repository”. Public repositories allow visitor Read access; private personal repositories allow access only to their owner and explicitly authorized subjects; private organization repositories allow access only to organization Owners, members with direct repository roles, or direct members of teams with repository roles, and ordinary organization Members do not automatically gain access merely through membership. After visibility or access grants change, search, lists, direct links, and repository pages must all use the same access rule."},{"req_id":"REQ-3-3","path":"fields.name","text":"View a Public Repository Overview"},{"req_id":"REQ-3-3","path":"fields.description","text":"The repository overview identifies a seeded public repository in a visible heading, displays a “Public” marker, and provides a navigation link “Code” distinct from the clone-menu Code button. The public repository is readable without sign-in and retains its heading after reload.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-repository-overview.png)"},{"req_id":"REQ-4","path":"fields.name","text":"Code and Version Control"},{"req_id":"REQ-4","path":"fields.description","text":"The Code page is the main page for browsing code in a repository — the top of the page displays the current branch selector, the main area displays files and directories at the current path on the current branch, clicking a file opens a read-only file page, and clicking Commits opens commit history. A file is content at a path on a branch; a directory is only a path hierarchy used for organization and is not an independent collaboration object. A branch is a named reference pointing to a commit, and switching branches only changes the file snapshot read by the current page. A commit is an immutable change record that stores the parent commit, author, message, time, and changed files; users with Write, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner permission can create new commits from a file page through Edit or Add file. Every file, commit, comparison, and branch page displays the repository and current branch or revision. Editing a file must create a new commit and must not rewrite historical content. Seed data for read-only scenarios consists of public repositories and directly openable repository, file, and commit pages; visitors need not sign in to browse files, history, diffs, code search, or existing branches. Write scenarios provide separate existing contributor accounts with Write or higher permission on their target repositories and an unprotected writable branch; default-branch scenarios provide an Admin and a separate readable non-Admin account. These accounts sign in through the home-page “Sign in” link, the “Username or email” and “Password” fields, and the “Sign in” button; the signed-in username is visible before opening the target repository entry. Unless a narrower scope is explicitly given below, each named control is unique on the active page, and field and option names refer to accessible names."},{"req_id":"REQ-4-1","path":"fields.name","text":"Browse Repository Files and Directories"},{"req_id":"REQ-4-1","path":"fields.description","text":"This feature builds on the public repository overview provided by REQ-3-3 (View a Public Repository Overview). A visitor with repository-view permission can use the Code page to browse the selected branch's directory hierarchy and open files without changing repository data. Directory and file entries are links with their exact accessible names; a directory identifies the current path and a file page displays the stored file name, path, branch context, and readable content. Seed data provides public repository `acme-docs`, directory `src`, text file `README.md`, and expected content `Document search flow`. Opening the directory and then the file displays that content, and reloading the file page preserves the same read-only content.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-code-file-browser.png)"},{"req_id":"REQ-4-2","path":"fields.name","text":"Commit History and Code Search"},{"req_id":"REQ-4-2","path":"fields.description","text":"The “commit history” page displays commit records for a branch or file path in reverse chronological order; the “diff” page compares the file contents of two commits or revisions line by line, where base is the earlier or target revision and compare is the newer or to-be-compared revision; the “code search” page searches for keywords only within readable file content in the current repository. All three are read-only views that do not create commits or modify files or branches and follow repository visibility and access permissions. This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes."},{"req_id":"REQ-4-2-1","path":"fields.name","text":"View Repository Commit History"},{"req_id":"REQ-4-2-1","path":"fields.description","text":"This feature builds on the repository and file browsing context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories). A user with repository-view permission can open the repository's commit history from its repository page and inspect the records for the readable branch. Each record represents an immutable change and may expose its commit identifier, author, time, parent, and changed files. The repository page exposes a history link named “Commits”; a commit count may accompany the label without creating another matching link. Seed history includes the message `Document search flow`, author `alice-dev`, and a relative timestamp containing “ago”. Opening branch history directly displays these values without requiring file editing or other write actions.

![image](reference/github-commit-diff.png)"},{"req_id":"REQ-4-2-3","path":"fields.name","text":"Search Code Within a Repository"},{"req_id":"REQ-4-2-3","path":"fields.description","text":"This feature builds on the repository browsing context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories). A visitor can search readable file content within public repository `acme-docs` using the repository Search box, press Enter, and select the “Code” results view. Search is read-only and remains scoped to the current repository; it does not create commits or modify files. The results view provides matching file entries and opens a selected file in its repository context. Seed data provides query `search flow`, matching file `README.md` with that text visible, and absent query `no-such-token`. A matching file displays the query text and retains its file link after reload. ![image](reference/github-repository-code-search.png)"},{"req_id":"REQ-4-3","path":"fields.name","text":"Branch Management"},{"req_id":"REQ-4-3","path":"fields.description","text":"The branch selector is the control at the top of the Code page that lists and switches branches; the system stores a unique name and current pointed-to commit for each branch. Creating a branch creates a new named reference at a specified base commit; it does not copy files or rewrite base history. The default branch is the branch read by default when opening the repository overview or a repository entry without a specified branch; it is not the only existing or writable branch. A branch name is 1 to 255 characters and may contain only ASCII letters, digits, `-`, `_`, `.`, and `/`; it must not end with `/` or `.`, and must not contain consecutive `..` or `//`; duplicate names, invalid names, or lack of permission must prevent branch creation. The selector is a unique button named “Branch <current branch name>”; it opens a textbox named “Find branch” and selectable options whose exact accessible names are branch names. As the user types, matching options or a “No matching branch” state update without requiring Enter or a separate search action. Seed data provides public repository `branch-switch-demo`, active branch `main`, target branch `feature-search`, target-only file `main-only.md`, and unknown query `missing-branch`. Branch names are 1–255 characters and may contain ASCII letters, digits, `-`, `_`, `.`, and `/`; names ending in `/` or `.`, containing `..` or `//`, duplicating an existing name, or submitted by an unauthorized user must be rejected. The editor exposes a “File name” field, a “File contents” textbox, a “Commit message” field, and a “Commit changes” button. New file paths cannot be empty, start with `/`, contain a `..` path segment, or conflict with an existing file or directory. Commit messages must contain 1–72 non-empty characters after trimming whitespace. Invalid submissions must leave file data, branch head, and commit history unchanged; an invalid path is reported as “Invalid file path”, while a missing message is reported as “Commit message is required”.
